extracted.intended_audience: scholars, students, and journalists interested in media studies, agenda-setting, and U.S. foreign policy reporting
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and criteria that determine which foreign-affairs events become news in Washington-centered press coverage; derived from Cohen's participant observation and interviews with reporters and officials. Useful for evaluating newsworthiness and press behavior in the foreign-policy domain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government-Source Privilege
rubrics_metrics.description: State Department, White House, and Congressional foreign-policy briefings supply most foreign-affairs news. Beats anchored to these institutions confer newsworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cohen observes that institutional access to official briefings effectively determines which stories reporters can produce; being on or near these beats grants a story higher likelihood of coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crisis Salience
rubrics_metrics.description: Crises (wars, coups, summits, treaties) command attention; quieter foreign developments are systematically under-covered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Events that present overt drama or immediate stakes attract disproportionate coverage compared with slow-moving or routine developments, producing systematic under-reporting of non-crisis issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bilateral US Relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Events involving US allies, US enemies, or US interests are vastly more reportable than events with no US connection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newsworthiness is filtered by the extent to which a foreign event can be framed as directly relevant to U.S. policy or national interests; distant or indirectly linked events receive less attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proximity to a Briefing Cycle
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that can be hooked to the daily State Department or White House briefing cycle achieve newsworthiness even when their substantive importance is modest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing matters: items that fit neatly into regular briefing schedules are more likely to be produced and broadcast regardless of deeper significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporter–Source Mutual Dependence
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters depend on officials for information; officials depend on reporters for publicity. Stories that serve both interests are preferentially produced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reciprocal relationship creates incentives to produce coverage that meets officials' needs for visibility and reporters' needs for access, shaping which angles and facts appear in print.

rubrics_metrics.name: Background-Briefing Leverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Off-the-record briefings shape framing; stories that align with official background framings face fewer hurdles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Officials' off-the-record framings provide interpretive scaffolding that reporters often adopt; stories consistent with these framings are easier to place and to protect from pushback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Travel-Pool Coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Presidential and diplomatic travel pools concentrate coverage on the leader's location; events elsewhere fade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Logistical concentration of reporters in travel pools amplifies events tied to leaders' locations while diminishing resources for geographically dispersed coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wire-Service Availability
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories already on AP/UPI wires receive high salience because they are pre-cleared by the wire's editorial process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wire copy acts as a force-multiplier: items distributed by major wire services become de facto news priorities for other outlets, increasing their national salience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observer (press role)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporting on what happens (the conventional news role).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One of three roles Cohen identifies for the foreign-affairs press; emphasizes descriptive, event-focused coverage as a primary function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participant (press role)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes an actor in the policy process (leak conduit, trial-balloon vehicle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists can actively shape policy dynamics by transmitting information (intentionally or not) that officials use; this role implies normative questions about responsibility and influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catalyst (press role)
rubrics_metrics.description: Coverage shapes both public agenda and elite discussion, even when reporters do not intend it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Media can trigger changes in public salience and elite agendas through selection and emphasis; the catalytic effect links reporting choices to broader political consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agenda-Setting Impact
rubrics_metrics.description: News selection determines public attention even when it does not change opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cohen's aphorism—'The press may not be successful much of the time in telling people what to think, but it is stunningly successful in telling its readers what to think about'—captures the principle that selection shapes salience independently of persuasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural Elite Bias in Foreign News
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because reporting is oriented around official sources and institutions, the resulting coverage systematically reflects elite viewpoints and institutional priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beat-Driven / Bureaucratic Phase of Production
rubrics_metrics.description: Cohen's observations about beat-driven news production prefigure later critiques (e.g., Fishman 1980) by highlighting how institutional beats structure coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The organization of reporting around institutional beats (e.g., State Department, White House) forms a production phase that conditions story selection, framing, and coverage depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical Foundation for Later Agenda-Setting Research
rubrics_metrics.description: Cohen's aphorism provided a conceptual foundation later operationalized by empirical studies (e.g., McCombs & Shaw 1972).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cohen's qualitative findings function as a conceptual rubric for evaluating agenda-setting effects and for designing empirical tests of how media salience maps onto public and elite attention.
